title: Future continuous, future perfect and future perfect continuous

sections.title: Future continuous: I will be doing
sections.content:
We can use the future continuous to talk about:
(i) something that is predicted to start before a particular point of future time, and that may continue after this point (often the result of a previous decision or arrangement):
• When it goes into orbit, the spacecraft will be carrying 30 kilos of plutonium.
• Anna will be helping us to organise the party.
(ii) a future activity that is part of the normal course of events or that is one of a repeated or regular series of events:
• Dr Lin will be giving the same talk in room 103 at ten next Thursday.
• Will you be driving to work, as usual?
We can often use either the future continuous or the present continuous when we talk about arranged activities or events in the future (see also Unit 10). Compare:
• We will be leaving for Istanbul at 7:00 in the evening. (timetabled; or … are leaving …) and
• When the race starts later this afternoon, the drivers will be hoping for drier weather than last year. (not … are hoping …; not reporting the details of a programme or timetable)

sections.title: Future continuous vs will to avoid suggesting willingness
sections.content:
When we don't want to indicate willingness, intention, invitation, etc., we prefer to use the future continuous instead of will. For example, if guests have stayed longer than you wanted, and you don't know when they are leaving, you might ask:
• Will you be staying with us again tonight? (asking about their plans) rather than
• Will you stay with us again tonight? (they might think this is an invitation)

sections.title: Future perfect and future perfect continuous: I will have done / I will have been doing
sections.content:
We use the future perfect to say that something will be ended, completed, or achieved by a particular point in the future:
• By the time you get home I will have cleaned the house from top to bottom.
• I'm sure his awful behaviour will soon have been forgotten. (= passive form)
The future perfect is also sometimes used for politeness in more formal contexts:
• I hope this email will have reassured you that no further action is required.
We use the future perfect continuous to emphasise the duration of an activity in progress at a particular point in the future:
• Next year I will have been working in the company for 30 years.
With both the future perfect and future perfect continuous we usually mention the future time (e.g. By the time you get home …, Next year …).

sections.title: Future/Future perfect continuous for present and past situations
sections.content:
The future continuous, future perfect and future perfect continuous can also be used to say what we believe or imagine is happening around now:
• We could ask to borrow Joe's car. He won't be using it today – he went to work by bike.
• Most people will have forgotten the fire by now.
• Tennis fans will have been queuing at Wimbledon all day to buy tickets.
We can use the future perfect continuous to say what we think was happening at a point in the past:
• Motorist Vicky Hao will have been asking herself whether speed cameras are a good idea after she was fined £100 last week for driving at 33 mph in a 30 mph zone.

exercises.question: We ___ in an hour or so, make sure your suitcase is packed.
exercises.hint: Ongoing activity at a future point (result of prior arrangement) → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be leaving
Use the present continuous (not will) for personal arrangements — things planned and agreed with someone else, typically noted in a diary. Will would suggest a spontaneous decision.

exercises.question: Without more cheap housing, families ___ the village and find homes in town.
exercises.hint: Predicted ongoing activity shortly → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be moving to
Predicted ongoing activity shortly → future continuous. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: Will ___ late at the office again? I want to know when to cook.
exercises.hint: Asking about an ongoing future activity (normal course of events) → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: you be working
Asking about an ongoing future activity (normal course of events) → future continuous.

exercises.question: Well, I ___ over the weekend if that will help.
exercises.hint: Future activity NOT happening → future continuous negative.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: won't be working
Future activity NOT happening → future continuous negative.

exercises.question: I ___ my car until next week, so you can borrow it if you like.
exercises.hint: Activity not in progress at future point → future continuous negative.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: won't be using
Activity not in progress at future point → future continuous negative.

exercises.question: Don't call at 8pm — we ___ (have) dinner then.
exercises.hint: Activity in progress at a specific future time → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be having
The future continuous (will be + -ing) describes an activity that will be in progress at a specific future moment. 'At 8pm' specifies the future point during which the action will be ongoing.

exercises.question: My grandad ___ a computer. He says he's very happy with his old typewriter.
exercises.hint: Simple refusal/fact about future → will + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: won't use
Simple refusal/fact about future → will + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: Is your suitcase very heavy? I ___ you a hand if you like.
exercises.hint: Offer made at the moment of speaking → will + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will give
Use will for a decision made at the moment of speaking — an on-the-spot response to a situation. This contrasts with be going to, which is used for decisions already made before the moment of speaking.

exercises.question: Dr Sankey ___ evidence at the trial of James Morgan next week.
exercises.hint: Planned ongoing activity in the future (normal course of events) → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be giving
Planned ongoing activity in the future (normal course of events) → future continuous. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: He's parked his car across our drive and says he ___. Shall I call the police?
exercises.hint: Refusal (willingness/intention negative) → will + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: won't move
Refusal (willingness/intention negative) → will + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: The two schools ___ to a single campus at the beginning of September.
exercises.hint: Scheduled/timetabled arrangement → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be moving
Use the present simple for fixed, programmed, or institutionally scheduled events (train departures, concert times, class timetables). These events are set by an external authority and cannot be changed by the speaker.

exercises.question: By the time you read this, I ___ (leave) for the airport.
exercises.hint: Completed before a future point ('by the time') → future perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have left
'By the time' + present simple signals the future perfect (will have + past participle). The leaving will be completed before the reading happens.

exercises.question: The weather forecast says that the rain … by the morning and tomorrow will be dry.
exercises.hint: Completed by a future point → future perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have cleared
Completed by a future point → future perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: The company is making a profit… By the end of the year they ___ their target.
exercises.hint: Completed achievement by future point → future perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have achieved
Completed achievement by future point → future perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: In two years' time Morneau … conference of some interest.
exercises.hint: Completed discovery by future point → future perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have discovered
Use the past simple when the time period is clearly completed. Even if the word today appears, if the period (morning, afternoon, the working day) is clearly over from the speaker's perspective, the past simple is correct.

exercises.question: I am confident that I … the report before the end of the week.
exercises.hint: Task completed by future deadline → future perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have finished
Task completed by future deadline → future perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: As delegates who arrived early … there have been some late changes to the programme.
exercises.hint: Something likely completed by now/soon → future perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have discovered
Something likely completed by now/soon → future perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Next year she ___ (teach) at this school for a decade.
exercises.hint: Duration up to a future point → future perfect continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have been teaching
The future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing) emphasises the duration of an ongoing activity up to a future point. 'A decade' signals the duration; 'next year' is the future endpoint.

exercises.question: I suppose by now school ___ for Christmas.
options: will close / will have closed → will have closed
will close / will had closed → will had closed
exercises.hint: Action completed by 'now' → future perfect (will have closed).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will close / will have closed → will have closed
Action completed by 'now' → future perfect (will have closed). The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: You ___ a rest.
options: will be enjoying / will have been enjoying → will be enjoying
will be enjoying / will have been enjoying → will be enjoyed
exercises.hint: Ongoing activity right now → future continuous (will be enjoying).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be enjoying / will have been enjoying → will be enjoying
This is the future perfect passive (will have been + past participle). Use it to describe an action that will be completed before a specific future moment, with the subject as the receiver of the action. The signal here is by + future time and a passive subject.

exercises.question: It's only a few months until he ___ school for college.
options: will be leaving / will have been leaving → will be leaving
will be leaving / will was leaving → will be leaving
exercises.hint: Event at a future point (about to leave) → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be leaving / will have been leaving → will be leaving
This is the future perfect passive (will have been + past participle). Use it to describe an action that will be completed before a specific future moment, with the subject as the receiver of the action. The signal here is by + future time and a passive subject.

exercises.question: My brother Joe and his family ___ next Friday.
options: will have been arriving / will be arriving → will be arriving
will had been arriving / will be arriving → will be arriving
exercises.hint: Arrival at a specific future time → future continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have been arriving / will be arriving → will be arriving
This is the future perfect passive (will have been + past participle). Use it to describe an action that will be completed before a specific future moment, with the subject as the receiver of the action. The signal here is by + future time and a passive subject.

exercises.question: By the time they get here they ___ to California and New Zealand.
options: will be going / will have been → will have been
would be going / would have been → would have been
exercises.hint: Completed experience by future point → future perfect (will have been).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will be going / will have been → will have been
Use the present perfect for life experience when no specific time is given. The focus is on whether the experience has happened, not when. If a specific time is mentioned (last year, in 2019), switch to the past simple.
